author: smimon
text:
Quick question for you pal - am I being overly optimistic in thinking it should be possible to spot the reason for every turn in the market?

I understand that the goal is to focus on only the most significant levels, trade edges etc for high probability, and I'm making some great trades like this. But sometimes, I see what to all intents and purposes appears to be an important FTR get taken out and a PAZ entered, only for price to then turn from a seemingly random place, and no matter how much I try to apply RTM reasoning and methodology to it, it simply doesn't make sense why it turned from where it did. I then get "stuck" with incorrect directional bias, expecting a PAZ to complete, which never does (although sometimes in fairness I've seen an incomplete PAZ move get completed days or even weeks later).

I put this down initially to inexperience, but I'm pretty confident in marking up the correct FLs on the charts now, and 9 times out of 10, even if I get something wrong, I understand why with hindsight. It's the 1 in 10 that's driving me nuts.

Much of what I see that confuses me can be explained if you consider the DP to engulf a FL/FTR an important level in its own right, but I was under the impression that it was only FTRs and the engulfs thereof that mattered in the scheme of things (assuming of course the DP isn't an important FL/FTR itself).

So two questions really - to clarify, is it only the FTR formed after an engulf, and not the DP to engulf that is important? And if so, why do we so often see big turning points take place from engulf DPs, when its corresponding FTR has been taken out?

And also, are there just times you have to shrug your shoulders, and move on? Or is it possible to understand every move?

All the best, thanks for any help.

author: smimon
text:
Apologies for posting again, but a chart always helps in these situations. Here's a chart of recent action on the Dax, M30, which I've annotated to highlight my confusion.

In this case, the DP to engulf was clearly a significant level in its own right, even though its corresponding FTR was engulfed. Things like this happening are the final thing that is preventing me from becoming highly consistent with my trading.

I've dropped down to M1 to see if I could see anything - I marked on the origin of the move down at (1) that was a reaction to the seemingly important FL:

And then zoomed into the area where the big bounce at 3 came from:

I know it's good practice to take profit at the first reasonable target, it's just that when this sort of thing happens it seems to invalidate the FTR theory (to my mind at least - I may well be wrong!) and then makes me second guess taking entries, or whether I should hold a trade or not.

At the moment I'm thinking I need to readjust my thinking - if we have a pole base which engulfed an important FL, and then a FTR which formed thereafter, I should only consider the "whole thing" engulfed if both the FTR and the pole base are taken out. If just the FTR is taken out, and not the pole base which contained the DP to engulf, then the zone is not dead.

Cheers

author: benhur
text:
Hi Smimon, and thank you for posting in my journal!!!

First you will have to excuse me I am not so used to name PA by names such as FTR DP etc... I simply trade HTF engulf with LTF confirmation.

It is very reasonable to understand each and every move. Of course we wouldn't want to trade them all - as they may lack good probability and R ratio, but after it happen I can reason 99% of turns and bounces.

I always use horizontal lines and drill up and down TF to provide explanations, and most of the time I see the amazing accuracy of the market. I learn with that process allot, and highly reccomand you add this continues learning into your routine. I am Trading with the Axiom every turn and bounce is explainable and accurate.

Few years ago I did try to whipsaw the market, trade each leg up 'n down. So it is very much possible, but also very exhausting. It's really important you can do that for the skill as it deeply make you one with the market. But it is not the efficient way of trading.

author: smimon
text:
Thanks for getting back to me pal. This week has been a big learning experience, in the sense that I've realised that whilst FTRs and their engulfs are the most important thing to watch, it's all got to be in the context of reading the bigger picture correctly. You've also got to consider HTF SR lines, and flags that become flip zones. A LTF engulf of a bullish zone means little, if we've just engulfed a huge bearish one just before a retrace.

I think I'm doing what you describe - trying to be on every single up and down move, and you're right - it is exhausting! But a necessary learning process. I've got a bit of an obsessive personality, so I'm determined to sit here until I understand the reason for everything I see before I go live with real cash, otherwise it's going to be a stressful experience.

All the best
